name: Wayampi
confidence_why: Copin's 2012 grammar of the Ytuwasu (Upper Oyapock) variety marks stress on the final syllable in every transcribed form and Carvalho's 2026 phonology of the Amapari variety describes ultimate accent as the rule, with penultimate accent only before unstressable enclitics such as locative -pɛ, while the penultimate stress Jensen 1999 attributes to Wayampi is the accentual retraction her 1984 study found in the Upper Jari dialect alone, so the apparent conflict is a dialect split and final stress is the clear reading for the varieties with full descriptions.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Wayampi with an empty rule and no existing statements; this source supplies a rule (final accent, PrWd domain) plus the exception classes, secondary prominence, and the dialect split (Upper Jari retracted vs Amapari/Ytuwasu final). Nothing to contradict since the catalog records no placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary accent falls on the final (rightmost) syllable of the Prosodic Word in Amapari Wajãpi; penultimate accent occurs when the last syllable is an unaccentable suffix/enclitic (e.g. locative -pɛ ~ -mɛ) or an unaccented final -a/-ɨ; secondary prominences appear in derived forms, compounds and some underived polysyllables. Amapari and Ytuwasu retain final accent; the Upper Jari dialect has retracted (penultimate) accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 19: "Forms from (b) to (d) illustrate, moreover, secondary prominences occurring in derived forms with bound elements (-katu 'to be good, in significant quantity'; in b), in compounds (with tɛʔa 'eye' and kuʔi 'dust, powder'; in c) and in basic, underived forms (d)." Examples: [iˌβɔkaˈtu] 'really right', [teˌʔakuˈʔi] 'conjunctivitis', [kaˌɾakuˈɾi] 'money'. The author cautions (p. 19) that "the accentual prominences discussed here depend, at this stage of the research, on auditory impressions only."
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate accent when the final syllable is an unaccentable suffix or enclitic: p. 20 "These are usually analyzable as involving morphological elaboration by means of suffixes or enclitics which cannot bear any accentuation, such as the locative -pɛ ∼ -mɛ"; p. 43 ɛ-ɾɛtã-pɛ [ɛɾɛˈtãmɛ] 'at my house' (locative 'apparently extrametrical', a clitic), versus completive -pa which 'attracts the main, word-level accent': a-aɾõ-pa [aɾõˈma] 'I have waited' (p. 44). Nouns with unaccented final -a (always nasalized) or -ɨ have penultimate accent: [tapiˈʔiɾã] 'tapir', [ˈɛɾã] 'his/her name', [ɨβɨˈtɨɾɨ] 'mountain' (p. 43). Dialect exception: Upper Jari has accent retraction, [ˈakɛ] 'I sleep', [ˈtata] 'fire' (citing Jensen 1984: 44), where Amapari has [aˈkɛ], [taˈta] (p. 20). Pronoun janɛ may be integrated into the noun's PrWd ([jaˌnɛɾẽˈtã]) or form its own ([jaˈne juˈɾu]) (p. 19).
new_statements.identity_note: de Carvalho 2026 describes the Amapari dialect (Brazil, Amapá) specifically, abbreviated AW; it states that the Ytuwasu variety shares final accent and that the Upper Jari variety (Jensen's main data) has retracted accent. A catalog rule 'fixed: final syllable' therefore applies to Amapari/Ytuwasu Wayampi; the Upper Jari dialect would be penultimate per Jensen 1984: 44 (unverified here).

new_statements.translation: [p. 29] ...in the proto-language the accent falls on the last syllable of the morpheme (Rodrigues' analysis, p.c.), which is the case in most languages of the family. [...] For Wayampi it would be necessary to propose one more rule, of accent shift before pause (#) (cf. A. Jensen 1979): SŚ → ŚS / ___ # ; *aké → áke 'I sleep', *tatá → táta 'fire'. [note 11, p. 44] In the Wayampi of the upper Jari, on which A. Jensen (1979) based his work, the accent shifts only when no suffix or enclitic follows. Accentuation was not recorded in the Wayampi data in this dissertation because of this alternation, and because no equivalent study has yet been made of the Amapari dialect.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Wayampi with an empty rule and no existing statements; this supplies a placement (pre-pausal penult, from underlying stem-final accent) for the Upper Jari dialect. It matches Olson & Olson 1975 (work 1, Jari dialect: penult in isolation). Carvalho 2026 (Amerindia 46, held by the project from an earlier reading, not in this item's list) cites exactly this note (Jensen 1984: 44) and reports that Amapari and Ytuwasu Wajãpi keep word-final accent ([aˈkɛ], [taˈta]), so the penult pattern is dialect-specific.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Inherited (Proto-Tupi-Guarani) accent is morpheme/stem-final; Wayampi (Upper Jari) has innovated a retraction rule that moves the accent to the penultimate syllable before pause, i.e. in words said in isolation or utterance-finally, but only when no suffix or enclitic follows the stem; otherwise the final (stem-final) accent surfaces. The thesis treats 'shift of the accent to the penultimate syllable' as one of the defining phonological changes of Wayampi (p. 47, p. 130) but deliberately does not mark accent in its data.
new_statements.exceptions: Retraction applies only pre-pausally and only when no suffix/enclitic follows (Upper Jari, after A. Jensen 1979 'Ritmo, acentuação e intonação em Oiampí'); no accent data for the Amapari dialect; accent not transcribed in the thesis data because of the alternation.
new_statements.identity_note: Olson & Olson 1975 is explicitly 'WAIAPĨ - Dialeto Jarí' (title page, June 1975); Jensen 1984's accent remarks rest on A. Jensen 1979 for the Wayampi of the alto Jari and she states no equivalent study existed for the Amapari dialect. The penult reading therefore describes the (Upper) Jari dialect of Wayampi; Amapari and Ytuwasu Wajãpi are reported elsewhere (Carvalho 2026) to have word-final accent.

Word-final syllables with /a/ or /ɔ/ 'seem to carry a slight explosive stress'. Statement is explicitly tentative and limited to isolation forms.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the works opened: Olson & Olson 1975 (Jari dialect) state penultimate stress for words in isolation, and Jensen 1984 describes the same thing diachronically as a Wayampi (Upper Jari) rule retracting the inherited stem-final accent to the penult before pause, applying only when no suffix or enclitic follows (so stem-final accent surfaces elsewhere); Moura & Olson 1978 is silent. Two qualifications the catalog should carry: (a) Olson notes final syllables with /a/ or /ɔ/ 'seem to carry a slight explosive stress'; (b) the pattern is dialect-bound: Jensen had no accent data for the Amapari dialect, and Carvalho 2026 (Amerindia 46, already held by the project from an earlier reading and not part of this item's list) reports word-final accent for Amapari and Ytuwasu Wajãpi ([aˈkɛ] 'I sleep', [taˈta] 'fire') and calls the penult retraction specific to Upper Jari. So for waya1270 as a whole the sources split by dialect: penult (pre-pausal, isolation forms) in Jari/Upper Jari vs final in Amapari/Ytuwasu; the catalog's empty rule is not contradicted by anything.

audit.recode_to: From 'descriptions disagree' to a dialect-resolved coding: languoid default (Upper Oyapock/Ytuwasu = Copin's reference-grammar variety, and Amapari = Carvalho) = fixed word-final (ultimate) accent on the prosodic word, weight-blind, R edge (01/001/0001), now source-STATED (Carvalho 2026:19-20 'the rightmost syllable of the domain'; 'Ytuwasu and AW varieties.. retain the PTG pattern of ultimate accentuation') rather than example-grade; exceptions = (i) unaccentable enclitics/suffixes such as locative -pɛ give surface penult (Carvalho 2026:20, 43; Copin fn.61), (ii) a lexical class of AW nouns with unaccented final -ã/-ɨ < PTG *-a ([ˈɛɾã], [tapiˈʔiɾã]; Carvalho 2026:43); dialect caution = Upper Jari has accent retraction (penult on unsuffixed stems; Jensen 1984:44, 1999:133). If the schema needs one languoid-wide value, variable-by-dialect is defensible, but 'descriptions disagree' is not: Carvalho 2026:20 reports that Jensen 1984 restricted retraction to Upper Jari and had no Amapari data, so no two sources contradict each other on the same variety.
